title: Your workspace
one: SSMS, Visual Studio and OneDrive inside the Programming Environment, and where your files live.
marks: This chapter earns no marks by itself. Every mark in the chapters after it depends on files that are saved in the right place, and on tools that open and connect.

screens.title: See what you will set up in this chapter.

blocks.p: Before you build anything, three things need to be in place. The first is a folder in your school OneDrive, where every file for this coursework lives. The second is SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS), connected to the database server. The third is Visual Studio 2019, checked so that it can make the kind of program this guide builds.

You do all of this inside the Programming Environment, the Windows desktop you are signed in to now. By the end of the chapter you will have run your first line of SQL, and one empty file called BikeShop.sql will be waiting in your own folder.

words: Programming Environment
The Windows desktop you reach through C2k, where SQL Server and the programming tools are installed.
OneDrive
Storage on your school account. A file saved there can be opened from any computer you sign in on.
Folder
A named place that holds files, the way a ring binder holds pages.
File Explorer
The Windows window that shows your folders and files.
Green tick
The mark OneDrive puts beside a file or folder once it has copied it to your school account.
SQL
The language you use to make a database and to ask it questions.
Database
A set of tables that keeps the shop's records, such as its customers and its bookings.
Server
A program that keeps databases and answers the SQL sent to it. It has no window of its own.
LocalDB
A small copy of SQL Server that starts by itself when a program connects to it.
SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS)
The window you use to type SQL, send it to the server, and read the answer.
Connect
Link SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) to one server, so that the SQL you type goes to that server.
Query
A question or an instruction written in SQL, such as a request for the server's version.
F5
The key that runs the SQL in the window. It does the same as the Execute button.
Script
A file of SQL lines that the server runs from the top to the bottom. Its name ends in .sql.
Visual Studio 2019
The program you use to build the shop's windows and buttons, and the C# code behind them.
C#
The programming language you use in class, written C and a hash sign and said C sharp.
Template
A ready-made starting point that Visual Studio 2019 fills in when you make a new project.
Project
The set of files that make one program.
Solution folder
The folder Visual Studio 2019 makes for your project, with every file of the program inside it.
bin and obj
Two folders Visual Studio 2019 makes each time it builds the program. They are made again from your code, so you leave them out when you hand in.
Zip
Pack a folder into one smaller file that can be handed in.

screens.title: Make your coursework folder in OneDrive.

blocks.p: Your coursework folder is called A2 SSD Coursework, and it sits inside OneDrive - C2k, your school OneDrive. OneDrive keeps a copy of everything in this folder on your school account. That means you can reach it from any computer you sign in on, and it is safe if one computer breaks. Every file you make in this guide goes in this folder: the script in chapter 1 and the program in chapter 5.

screens.title: Open SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) and connect it to the database server.

blocks.p: SQL Server is the program that keeps your database. It runs quietly in the background and has no window of its own. SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) is the window you use to talk to it: you type SQL, press F5, and the server's answer appears underneath.

The server in the Programming Environment is called `(localdb)\mssqllocaldb`. It is LocalDB, a small copy of SQL Server that starts by itself when SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) connects to it. You type this name once each time you open SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS), so it is worth getting every character right: the brackets, the backslash, and no spaces.

screens.title: Run your first line of SQL, which asks the server for its version.

blocks.p: A query is a question or an instruction written in SQL. You type it in a query window and press F5 to run it. Your first query is one line: `SELECT @@VERSION;` Type it exactly, with two at signs and a semicolon at the end.

Each part of the line has a job. SELECT means show me. @@VERSION is a value the server always knows about itself: its own name and version number. The two at signs mark it as one of the server's own values. The semicolon ends the instruction, the way a full stop ends a sentence. If one row comes back, SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) is connected and the server is answering.

steps.do: Click New Query on the toolbar, or press Ctrl and N together.
steps.see: A tab named SQLQuery1.sql opens with an empty white window, and the cursor blinks in it.

Type into the empty window.

steps.do: Type `SELECT @@VERSION;` in the empty window.
steps.see: The line reads `SELECT @@VERSION;` with SELECT coloured blue and @@VERSION coloured pink.

steps.do: Press F5 to run the query.
steps.see: A Results tab opens under the window with one row. Its one box holds a long line that starts with Microsoft SQL Server, then a year and a version number. The bar at the bottom says Query executed successfully.

img.alt: A query window in SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) holding the line SELECT @@VERSION; with the Results tab underneath showing one row. Its one box starts with Microsoft SQL Server, then a year and a version number. The bar at the bottom says Query executed successfully.
img.cap: Your first query and its answer. One row came back from the server, so SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) is connected and working.

Red text that says 'Incorrect syntax near'
A character is missing or extra. Compare your line with `SELECT @@VERSION;` character by character, then press F5 again.

blocks.p: This query window becomes your script. A script is a file of SQL lines that the server runs from the top to the bottom, and its name ends in .sql. screens.title: Open Visual Studio 2019 and check that the Windows Forms template is there.

blocks.p: Visual Studio 2019 is where you build the program that the shop's staff use: the windows, the buttons and the C# code behind them. You make that program in chapter 5. Today you check one thing. The Programming Environment must have the template this guide uses, which is Windows Forms App (.NET Framework) for C#. A template is a ready-made starting point that Visual Studio 2019 fills in for a new project. You look for it, then go back without making anything.

stages.title: What you hand in and the home note

screens.title: Read the list of what you hand in at the end.

blocks.p: From this guide you hand in two things, and both are made in your A2 SSD Coursework folder, so nothing has to be found or copied at the last minute. Your write-up is handed in as well, and it is taught separately.

box.title: The two things you hand in from this guide
box.text: The first is BikeShop.sql, the script that makes your database. The second is the BikeShop solution folder from Visual Studio 2019, zipped into one file, with its bin and obj folders left out.

blocks.p: Visual Studio 2019 makes the bin and obj folders every time it builds your program. They are large, and they are made again from your code, so the examiner does not need them. You zip the solution folder once, at the very end, when the program is finished.

To zip it, close Visual Studio 2019 first. Open File Explorer, open your A2 SSD Coursework folder, then open the BikeShop solution folder inside it, then open the BikeShop project folder inside that, which is the one that holds the bin and obj folders. Delete the folder named bin and the folder named obj. Go back to A2 SSD Coursework, right-click the BikeShop solution folder, point at Send to, and click Compressed (zipped) folder. A file named BikeShop.zip appears beside the folder, and that is the file you hand in.

screens.title: Read when to run your script.

blocks.p: From chapter 3 onward, BikeShop.sql makes your whole database: the tables, the sample data, and later the stored procedures, which are named blocks of SQL saved in the database. The database it makes lives on the server `(localdb)\mssqllocaldb` inside the Programming Environment, not in your OneDrive folder. The script is the part that lives in OneDrive.
When you sign out of the Programming Environment, the database on the server may be gone the next time you sign in. The box below says what to do about it, and it is the same for every chapter.

box.title: When to run your script
box.text: BikeShop.sql is the master copy of your database. At the start of every session, open it in SQL Server Management Studio: click File, point at Open, click File…, and double-click BikeShop.sql in your OneDrive coursework folder. Then press F5 with nothing highlighted. It takes two seconds. Chapter 3 shows you how to make SQL Server Management Studio write a script of the whole database, called BikeShop-saved.sql. From chapter 7, when your tests leave rows you need next lesson, you save that script before you log off and run it instead. Chapter 7 shows you when.

screens.title: Read what changes if you work at home.

blocks.p: Some pupils install SQL Server Express, SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) and Visual Studio 2019 on a computer at home. If you do, one thing changes, which is the server name. At home the server is your own, such as `.\SQLEXPRESS`. The full stop before the backslash means this computer, and SQLEXPRESS is the name SQL Server Express gives itself when it installs.

box.title: If you work at home
box.text: Type your own server name in the Server name box when SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) asks you to connect. In chapter 5 you write the server name a second time, in a settings file called App.config, and at home you change it there too. The database at home is a separate one, so run BikeShop.sql there to make it. Nothing else changes: the script, the code and the steps in this guide are the same.

stages.title: Prove it: your workspace is ready

screens.title: Tick the table: the folder, the script, the server and the template.

blocks.p: Every row below is a check you do now, in the Programming Environment. Two rows are mistakes made on purpose, and a refusal there is a pass, not a fail: it proves that SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) is talking to a real server that checks what you send it.

check.what: Your coursework folder is in OneDrive with a green tick
check.how: Press the Windows key and E together, and click OneDrive - C2k on the left. You see A2 SSD Coursework in the list, with a green tick in the Status column.

check.what: BikeShop.sql is saved in the folder
check.how: Double-click A2 SSD Coursework in File Explorer. You see BikeShop.sql in it, with a green tick beside it.

check.what: A wrong server name is refused
check.how: Close SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) with the cross at its top right. Start it again from the Start menu. In the Server name box type `(localdb)\mssqllocal`, with the last two letters missing, and click Connect. After a few seconds a red box names a network-related or instance-specific error, and nothing connects. Click OK.
In the same Connect to Server box, type `(localdb)\mssqllocaldb` in the Server name box and click Connect. Object Explorer shows `(localdb)\mssqllocaldb` with a Databases folder under it.

check.what: The server answers your first query
check.how: Click New Query, type `SELECT @@VERSION;` and press F5. The Results tab shows one row that starts with Microsoft SQL Server.
Press Ctrl and A in the same window, type `SELECT @@VERSIO;` with the N missing, and press F5. The Messages tab shows red text: Must declare the scalar variable "@@VERSIO". Nothing else happens.

check.what: The Windows Forms template is there
check.how: Start Visual Studio 2019, click Create a new project, and type Windows Forms in the search box. You see Windows Forms App (.NET Framework) with C# under its name. Click Back and close Visual Studio 2019.

blocks.p: Seven ticks mean your workspace is ready. Close the query window without saving it, because the test lines in it are not part of your script. Click the cross on its tab, which is named SQLQuery1.sql, above the white window. When SQL Server Management Studio asks whether to save changes, click No, or Don't Save if that is the word on the button. Your one saved file, BikeShop.sql, is empty and waiting in your OneDrive folder. Chapter 3 opens it and fills it with the tables.
